lines.text: Aarav says he doesn't want engineering. He acts accordingly — he works at the shop, he supports his family, he doesn't apply.
His beliefs, desires, and actions are perfectly consistent. By the standard of thin rationality, there is nothing wrong.
But I watched those beliefs form. I watched the notebook close. I watched the ambition shrink.
The question is not whether he acts on what he wants. The question is whether what he wants was shaped by conditions that gave him no real choice.

Thin rationality checks for consistency. Broad rationality checks for formation. A person can pass the first test — their actions match their preferences — while failing the second — their preferences were never freely formed.
This is the test that won't let us rest.

Elster's nine mechanisms are tools of broad rationality. They ask: was this preference produced by learning and reflection, or by deprivation and constraint? Thin rationality cannot tell the difference. Broad rationality demands that we look.
